openers.what-soil-is-made-of: Soil is built from two very different materials. One is mineral: naturally occurring solids, each with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure. Weathering supplies them, breaking rock apart by force or remaking it through chemistry, as when iron in a mineral changes from Fe2+ to Fe3+. The other is soil organic matter: plant and animal remains at various stages of decay, soil microbes and the substances they make. Climate decides how much of it builds up, and together it forms a large carbon store that can take carbon in or give it back.

soil-found-045.title: Soil organic matter, the once-living part of soil
soil-found-045.text: Most upland topsoils are only 1% to 6% organic material by mass, yet that thin share does an outsized amount of work. Soil organic matter is the organic part of soil. It takes in plant and animal remains at various stages of decay, the cells and tissues of soil microbes, and the substances those microbes make. It has three parts. The first is living microbial biomass. The second is dead material, fresh and partly decomposed. The third is more stable organic carbon. Fresh litter lying on the surface is usually left out. Amounts vary enormously. Deserts hold under 1%, while low-lying wet soils can reach 90%. Soils with 12% to 18% organic carbon are generally classed as organic soils. It is usually estimated to be 58% carbon, so a measurement of the organic carbon in a soil often stands in for it. Its benefits are many. It helps grains clump into crumbs, and improves water retention and biodiversity, holds back pollutants and buffers the soil against change. It also raises fertility. It offers sites that hold positively charged nutrients, and stores nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and micronutrients that microbes release slowly. How much builds up, and of what kind, depends on the kind of soil, which is set by the forces described in {{ref:soil-form-043}}. It is one ingredient of the mix described in {{ref:soil-found-078}}.

soil-found-029.title: Minerals, the crystals that build rock and soil
soil-found-029.text: As of August 2026, the International Mineralogical Association recognized 6,228 official mineral species. A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure. That last condition matters. Opal and obsidian are natural solids with no definite crystal structure, so they are more properly called mineraloids. Structure can even split one compound in two. Quartz and stishovite are both silicon dioxide, yet they count as two species. A mineral must also form by natural geological processes. That rule excludes purely human-made products, and biological ones such as seashells. A rock is something else: a bulk solid geologic material made of one mineral or an aggregate of several. Mineralogists classify minerals by their key chemical constituents, chiefly in the Dana and Strunz systems. One family dominates. The minerals described in {{ref:soil-found-031}} make up approximately 90% of the Earth's crust. In soil, minerals form the gritty bulk. The sand and silt fractions are mostly inert rock particles such as quartz, calcite, feldspar and mica.

soil-found-052.title: Weathering: how solid rock starts becoming soil
soil-found-052.text: Sedimentary rock covers 66% of the continents, and all of it is made from rock that was broken down first. That breakdown is weathering: the decay of rocks, soils and minerals through contact with water, atmospheric gases, sunlight and living things. Weathering happens in place. That sets it apart from erosion, where water, ice, wind, waves or gravity carry rock and mineral material away. It comes in two kinds. One is physical, the mechanical breakdown of rock by heat, water, ice and wind. The other is chemical, the reaction of rock with water, gases and biological chemicals. Water drives both, though oxygen and carbon dioxide from the air, and the activities of organisms, also matter. The two kinds work as a team. Cracks widened by force expose more surface to chemical attack, which speeds disintegration. The material left behind then combines with organic material, the {{ref:soil-found-045}}, to create soil. Weathering is a crucial part of the rock cycle, and it begins with the solids described in {{ref:soil-found-029}}.

soil-found-050.title: Why cold and waterlogged soils hoard organic matter
soil-found-050.text: Cold and standing water are the soil's preservatives. Climate, chiefly temperature and moisture, strongly controls how this material is produced, built up and broken down in soil. Temperature, soil moisture and topography are the main factors in how much of the {{ref:soil-found-045}} accumulates. Where cold slows the decomposers, it piles up. Waterlogging does the same by making the soil anaerobic, or short of oxygen. The tropics show the reverse. Heavy rain and heat speed decomposition and wash nutrients away, so forests there depend on living biomass recycling nutrients efficiently. Slope matters too. On steep cultivated slopes, erosion strips the topsoil, which holds most of the raw organic material that would otherwise become stable organic carbon.

soil-found-049.title: The soil's carbon store, bigger than the air's
soil-found-049.text: Soil holds an estimated 2,500 gigatons of carbon. That is 3.3 times the 750 gigatons in the atmosphere and 4.5 times the 560 gigatons in all living things. About 1,550 gigatons of it is organic carbon, mostly in soil organic matter. The rest is inorganic carbon, mainly carbonates and bicarbonates. This pool is never still. Gains and losses keep it in dynamic equilibrium, so soil can take carbon up or release it as greenhouse gas emissions. Soil can hold carbon for centuries to millennia. That is why the way people manage soil organic matter matters for slowing climate change.

soil-found-058.title: Chemical weathering: rock remade for life at the surface
soil-found-058.text: Most rock is born hot and squeezed. It forms at high temperature and pressure, so its minerals are often unstable in the cool, wet, oxidizing conditions at the Earth's surface. Chemical weathering is the result. Water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock and change its composition. It does three things at once. It turns some primary minerals, the ones the rock formed with, into new secondary minerals. It carries other substances off in solution. And it leaves the most stable minerals unchanged, as a resistate. Water is the main agent. Through the reactions in {{ref:soil-found-060}}, it turns many primary minerals into fine sheet minerals or hydrated oxides. Oxygen oxidizes minerals, and carbon dioxide drives carbonation. The new set of minerals sits closer to equilibrium with surface conditions. True equilibrium is rare, though, because water keeps washing the dissolved products away. Chemical weathering is usually much more important than the mechanical kind in {{ref:soil-found-053}}. Mountains show its reach. Uplift exposes fresh rock to air and moisture, releasing calcium and other ions into surface waters.

soil-found-063.title: Lichens, roots and microbes that wear down rock
soil-found-063.text: Two common minerals, albite and muscovite, weather twice as fast in live soil as in sterile soil. Living things make the difference. Biological weathering is weathering started or sped up by soil microorganisms, lichens and plant roots. Soil organisms make up about 10 mg/cm3 of typical soils. Lichens are among the most effective agents. In a New Jersey study, hornblende granite under lichen weathered three to four times faster than bare rock. Most commonly, plants release carbon dioxide along with chelating compounds, chemicals that grip metal ions, such as organic acids and siderophores. Roots can raise carbon dioxide to 30% of all soil gases. The chelating acids strip metal ions, especially aluminum and silicon, from rock. Where they build up, they can reshape whole soils. Partnerships help too. Root-dwelling fungi free nutrients from minerals such as apatite or biotite and pass them to trees, and some bacteria weather minerals in ways that promote plant growth. Life also works by force. Seedlings and roots growing in crevices push rock apart, and lichens pluck mineral grains loose with their hyphae, their thread-like filaments.

soil-found-059.title: Dissolution: when a mineral vanishes into water
soil-found-059.text: Some minerals leave nothing behind when they weather. In dissolution weathering, also called simple or congruent dissolution, a mineral dissolves completely and no new solid forms. Rainwater easily dissolves soluble minerals such as halite and gypsum. Given enough time, it dissolves even quartz, which goes into solution as silicic acid. Limestone meets a special version. Rainwater and carbon dioxide form weak carbonic acid, which turns limestone into soluble calcium bicarbonate. Cold water holds more dissolved carbon dioxide, so this carbonate dissolution is favored at low temperature. That makes it important in glacial weathering. Pollution sharpens the attack. Unpolluted rain has a pH of around 5.6, where lower numbers mean more acid. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides make acid rain that can lower it to 4.5 or even 3.0.

soil-found-061.title: Oxidation weathering: iron that reddens and weakens rock
soil-found-061.text: A reddish-brown crust on a rock is often a sign of iron changing inside it. Oxidation weathering is chemical weathering by oxidation of metals in minerals, most commonly iron changing from Fe2+ to Fe3+. Oxygen and water drive the change. They turn Fe2+ into Fe3+ oxides and hydroxides such as limonite. The new surface crumbles easily, and the rock beneath grows weaker. Sulfide minerals oxidize too. Chalcopyrite, for example, turns to copper hydroxide and iron oxides, leaving colored deposits. The process reaches into the soil. Oxidizing primary minerals, especially sulfides and those containing Fe2+, generates soil acidity.

soil-found-053.title: Physical weathering: breaking rock without changing it
soil-found-053.text: A rock can be shattered into pieces that are chemically identical to the original. That is physical weathering, also called mechanical weathering or disaggregation: breaking rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry. Most of it comes from expansion and contraction as temperature changes, as in freeze–thaw and thermal fracturing. Unloading, the loss of weight from rock above, is the exception, since it works without any temperature change. Ice is the most important agent, as {{ref:soil-found-054}} explains. Next comes wedging by plant roots, which enter cracks and pry them apart. Burrowing worms and other animals help, and lichens pluck grains loose. Physical weathering is usually much less important than chemical weathering. In subarctic or alpine settings, though, it can be significant.

soil-found-048.title: What fallen leaves and roots are made of
soil-found-048.text: Fresh plant debris is mostly water, 60% to 90% of it. Dry it, and carbon, oxygen and hydrogen make up about 92% of the weight. The rest includes nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur, calcium, magnesium and trace nutrients. Its organic compounds range from simple sugars to cellulose, along with fats, nitrogen-bearing proteins and lignins from older woody parts. This debris is the raw material of {{ref:soil-found-045}}. One leftover stands apart. Charcoal, the elemental carbon left by incomplete burning, is highly resistant to decomposition.

soil-found-046.title: Most soil carbon lies below the top 20 cm
soil-found-046.text: About 70% of the organic carbon in the world's soils lies deeper than 20 cm. The surface layer has higher carbon concentrations. Deeper soil still stores more overall, because there is far more of it by mass. Radiocarbon dates show the carbon growing older with depth, a sign that deep soil keeps it longer. The forces at work change too. Living things shape organic carbon near the surface, while minerals take over at depth, binding carbon as {{ref:soil-found-047}}.

soil-found-054.title: Frost weathering and the ice that splits rock
soil-found-054.text: Water expands 9.2% when it freezes. Inside rock, the pressure this creates has a realistic upper limit of 14 megapascals, far above granite's tensile strength of about 4 megapascals. Frost weathering is physical weathering caused by ice forming inside rock outcrops. Frost wedging, the classic explanation, was long believed the main mechanism. It needs small, twisting cracks in almost saturated rock and daily freeze–thaw cycles. Those conditions are unusual, so it is unlikely to matter in the tropics, polar regions or arid climates. Growing theoretical and experimental work now favors ice segregation instead, though the question is still open. Water drawn to growing ice lenses can exert up to ten times the pressure of frost wedging. Ice segregation works best between −4 and −15 °C.

soil-found-062.title: Mineral hydration, water's first grip on a crystal
soil-found-062.text: Before water can take a crystal apart, it has to attach to it. In mineral hydration, water molecules, or H+ and OH− ions, attach rigidly to the atoms of a mineral. Iron oxides turning into iron hydroxides, and anhydrite hydrating to gypsum, are examples. Bulk hydration matters less than dissolution, hydrolysis and oxidation. But hydration of the crystal surface is the crucial first step in hydrolysis. Water at a fresh surface splits into H+ and OH−. Protons then replace the positive ions at the surface, freeing them. Loosened bonds release silicic acid and aluminum hydroxides. In feldspar, this starts at defects on the crystal surface, in a layer only a few atoms thick.

soil-found-056.title: Pressure release: rock that peels as it rises
soil-found-056.text: Granite and other intrusive rocks form deep underground, under great pressure. When erosion strips away the rock above, their outer parts expand. This is pressure release weathering, also called unloading. The expansion opens fractures parallel to the surface, and sheets of rock break away along them. Geologists call this exfoliation or sheeting. Where rock is buttressed, the stress toward the free surface can reach 35 megapascals, easily enough to shatter rock. A retreating glacier can do the same by lifting its weight off the rock beneath.

soil-found-057.title: Salt weathering: crystals that pry rock apart
soil-found-057.text: Salt can split stone. In salt weathering, also called haloclasty, salty water seeps into cracks and evaporates, leaving salt crystals that grow there. Like ice lenses, the grains draw in more dissolved salt through tiny gaps. They grow into lenses that press hard on the surrounding rock. Sodium and magnesium salts work best. Salt weathering happens wherever evaporation concentrates salts, so it is most common in arid climates and along coasts. In sedimentary rock, weathering of pyrite to iron(II) sulfate and gypsum can grow salt lenses too.

soil-found-055.title: Thermal stress: rock cracked by heat and cold
soil-found-055.text: Rock swells as it warms and shrinks as it cools, and the strain adds up. Thermal stress weathering is weathering caused by these temperature changes. It takes two forms. In thermal shock, which is uncommon, rock cracks at once. In the more typical thermal fatigue, repeated cycles of stress gradually weaken it. Deserts, with their large day–night swings, are the classic setting. Yet any large temperature change can drive it, including wildfire, so it is likely as important in cold climates. It works best when heated rock is buttressed by surrounding rock and can expand in only one direction. Its reputation has swung. Geologists long discounted it after early 20th-century oven experiments. Those experiments have since been criticized as unrealistic, and geomorphologists now re-emphasize the process.
